web_title: 7. Why the Price Is What It Is: Valuation, Reverse DCF & Peer Comps
book_title: Chapter 7: Why the Stock Trades Here — Market Expectations vs. Peers
question: What growth and margin recovery does $66.28 already price in, and how does Mondelez stack up against Hershey, PepsiCo, General Mills, and Kraft Heinz?

epigraph.quote: Price is what you pay; value is what you get. Discipline means waiting for the market to offer a margin of safety rather than paying full fair value into overhead resistance.
epigraph.author: Institutional Valuation Desk

web_blocks.html: At the November 20, 2026 close of $66.28, Mondelēz International has an $83.90 billion market cap and a $104.62 billion enterprise value [30]. Trailing twelve-month earnings stand at $3.17 per share. The stock trades at 20.89x TTM P/E and 19.76x Forward P/E [30][39]. It also trades at 12.03x EV/EBITDA, 2.62x EV/Sales, and 22.94x P/FCF (a 4.36% FCF yield), with a 3.05% dividend yield ($2.02 TTM) [30].

Historical multiples explain why the stock is fairly valued rather than cheap at CMP. Over the past five years, Mondelēz averaged a 23.46x trailing P/E [35]. Its ten-year average P/E sits between 21.34x and 23.84x [35][36]. During the 2024 cocoa spike, the stock de-rated to 17.36x in December 2024 [35]. Shares have rallied +23.13% YTD on Q3 2026's volume inflection (+1.8 pp) and margin recovery [37][38]. Wall Street consensus targets sit at $70.42, offering only +6.2% upside from $66.28 (0.85:1 R:R vs. our $61.43 stop) [30].

web_blocks.caption: Reverse DCF Deconstruction: What $66.28 Already Assumes (Base WACC 7.5%, Terminal Growth 2.5%)
web_blocks.takeaway: Grounded in MDLZ's 16.2% FY24 adjusted OM peak and $3.60B FY23 FCF peak (net of $1.2B ERP SG&A through 2028), a realistic Base Case yields $71.50 (21.0x $3.40 FY27E EPS)—leaving only 1.08:1 R:R at CMP $66.28, but 2.28:1 on a pullback to $64.50.

web_blocks.html: Three overhangs keep our Base Case grounded near consensus ($70.42–$71.50) rather than assuming an immediate 17.8% operating margin. First, MDLZ's 10-year historical adjusted operating margin peaked at 16.2% in FY2024, and $1.2 billion of ERP implementation expenses weigh on SG&A through 2028 [10][27]. Second, 9M 2026 payouts ($2.8B) exceeded 9M FCF ($1.66B) by $1.14B, limiting debt-free buyback acceleration [12][29]. Third, in a 5.04% 10-year Treasury environment with a 2.73x PEG ratio, multiple expansion above 21.0x requires sustained developed-market volume recovery [30].

web_blocks.title: Valuation Synthesis: Wait for Pullback Asymmetry ($63.35–$64.50)
paragraphs: At CMP $66.28, a grounded Base Target of $71.50 (21.0x $3.40 normalized FY27E EPS) offers only 1.08:1 reward-to-risk against our $61.43 stop (and 0.85:1 at $70.42 consensus). Waiting for a pullback into the $63.35–$64.50 support shelf restores reward-to-risk to 2.28:1 ($7.00 upside vs. $3.07 risk at $64.50), clearing our 1.50:1 hurdle.

web_blocks.html: What Changes the Valuation View: A pullback to $63.35–$64.50 restores >2.2:1 asymmetry to $71.50; conversely, FY27E EPS slipping below $3.25 or Adjusted Gross Margin stalling below 35.5% compresses fair value toward $55.00–$56.50.

book_paragraphs: Now that we have spent six chapters inside Mondelēz's factories, distribution trucks, cocoa hedging books, and ten-year cash flow statements without looking at the ticker tape, it is time to lift the veil and ask the single hardest question in investing: does $66.28 a share offer enough margin of safety to commit new capital today?

At $66.28 as of the November 20, 2026 close, you and I are looking at an $83.90 billion equity market capitalization and a $104.62 billion enterprise value, which incorporates $19.08 billion of net debt and $1.32 per share of cash. On trailing twelve-month earnings of $3.17 per share, the market is asking us to pay 20.89 times trailing earnings, 19.76 times forward earnings, 12.03 times enterprise value to EBITDA, 2.62 times enterprise value to sales, and 22.94 times free cash flow—a 4.36% free cash flow yield—while paying us a 3.05% trailing dividend yield ($2.02 per share trailing; $2.04 forward estimate).

When we place $66.28 against Mondelēz's own ten-year history and Wall Street's $70.42 consensus target, a sobering reality check emerges. Over the last five years, Mondelēz has traded at an average P/E of 23.46x, and over the past decade between 21.34x and 23.84x. Even so, Mondelēz's 10-year adjusted operating margin peaked at 16.2% in FY2024, and its peak annual free cash flow was $3.60 billion in FY2023. With $1.2 billion of ERP implementation expenses running through SG&A through 2028 and 10-year Treasury yields sitting at 5.04%, projecting a sudden jump to 17.8% operating margins and $4.15 billion of free cash flow would be wishful thinking.

Instead, let us ground our Base Case in Mondelēz's actual historical ceiling. Assuming 3.8% annual revenue growth, a normalized 16.5% adjusted operating margin (30 basis points above FY2024's 16.2% peak as cocoa normalizes), and $3.55 billion of steady-state free cash flow, FY2027E normalized earnings power reaches roughly $3.40 per share. Applying a realistic 21.0x forward multiple—in line with the 21.34x ten-year Macrotrends average—yields a Base Case target of $71.50 per share, closely aligned with Wall Street's $70.42 consensus.

Here is why valuation discipline matters so much at $66.28. Against our hard invalidation stop at $61.43 (-$4.85 risk), a $71.50 target from $66.28 offers only $5.22 of price upside—a 1.08-to-1 reward-to-risk ratio (and just 0.85-to-1 at $70.42 consensus). That fails our 1.50-to-1 minimum asymmetry hurdle. However, if we exercise patience and wait for a pullback into the $63.35–$64.50 support shelf near the 10-week EMA ($64.31) and 50-day SMA ($63.00), our risk drops to $3.07 per share while upside expands to $7.00—restoring reward-to-risk to an attractive 2.28-to-1.

Against its US packaged-food peers, Mondelēz's business quality still stands out. Hershey trades at $175.48 (19.84x trailing P/E, 18.57x forward P/E, 13.17x EV/EBITDA) with higher leverage (1.11x debt-to-equity versus MDLZ's 0.84x) and sits in a Stage 1 consolidation (-3.93% over the past year). PepsiCo trades at $140.54 (17.66x trailing P/E, 11.64x EV/EBITDA) with 2.33x debt-to-equity and a -3.81% one-year return. General Mills ($35.74, -25.25% 1Y) and Kraft Heinz ($25.39, +1.64% 1Y) are both nursing negative trailing GAAP ROE and net margins. Mondelēz is the cleanest operator in the group, which is precisely why we want to own it—just at $63.35–$64.50 rather than chasing $66.28.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION: Respecting Both the Historical Ceiling and the Asymmetry Hurdle
book_callouts.quote: A great business does not become a great buy at any price; when CMP upside to fair value is only 1.08-to-1, patience is an active portfolio decision.
book_callouts.text: By refusing to inflate our operating margin assumptions past Mondelēz's 16.2% historical peak, we see clearly why $66.28 is a WAIT_FOR_SUPPORT setup—and why $63.35–$64.50 is the exact price where risk-reward snaps back to 2.28-to-1.

book_subsections.title: Why We Reject Heroic Margin Assumptions: The ERP & Refinancing Bridge
paragraphs: Let us pause and walk through why an analyst must never stretch a steady-state operating margin assumption just to make a stock look cheap. In FY2024—before the full brunt of peak cocoa hedges hit the income statement—Mondelēz's adjusted operating margin peaked at 16.2%, and its peak annual free cash flow was $3.60 billion in FY2023. Over the next several years through 2028, management is executing a $1.2 billion enterprise resource planning (ERP) system overhaul whose implementation costs flow largely through SG&A.

At the same time, Mondelēz carries $21.21 billion of total debt ($19.08 billion net debt) on its balance sheet, including low-coupon Euro notes (0.25% to 2.375%) that will gradually refinance into a higher-rate environment where 10-year US Treasury yields sit at 5.04%. Factoring in both the ongoing ERP drag and realistic refinancing costs, modeling a 16.5% normalized operating margin and $3.55 billion of steady-state free cash flow is honest, achievable, and defensible. It does not require miracles, and it shows why waiting for $63.35–$64.50 gives us a genuine margin of safety.

book_subsections.title: Peer Valuation & Stage Reconciliation
paragraphs: One quick technical note on our peer comparison table so you are never confused by conflicting screener labels: in TradingView's short-term snapshot, PepsiCo, General Mills, and Kraft Heinz screen as Stage 2 because of brief moving-average crossovers, whereas our daily market-facts ledger classifies PepsiCo and General Mills as Stage 1 consolidations and Kraft Heinz as Stage 3. Regardless of the short-term label, Mondelēz's +18.89% one-year return, +23.13% year-to-date gain, and clean Q3 2026 volume/mix inflection put it in a league of its own among US packaged-food peers.
